place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 药园 · 这一年
place.en: Chending Temple · The herb garden · That year

setup.zh: 饭堂里有人说你偷药园炼丹，周衡翻开巡夜簿：「要说他偷，拿赃来。」可观里起了一句更要命的话：沈小满手里有丹，好丹。这句话，传到了丹房。
setup.en: Someone in the dining hall says you rob the herb garden to make pills; Zhou Heng opens the night-watch book: "If you say he stole, bring the stolen goods." But a deadlier line goes round the temple: Shen Xiaoman has pills, good ones. The line reaches the pill house.

recap.zh: 饭堂里说你偷药园的灵草炼丹，周衡翻开巡夜簿：「药园，一株不少。残株是巡夜的工钱，执事堂的牌子上写着……要说他偷，拿赃来。」私下只说一句：孙二狗那颗，「我看了。二转。」观里传开「沈小满手里有丹，好丹」，传到了丹房：守了三十年炉子的闵丹师叫你去，拿一颗看——数到第二道停了：「二转。这一颗，比我炉里的好。」闻了三回：「这丹，不是炉里出来的。没有火气。」你说是秘境里一个死人袋子里的；他不问第二遍，只说：「明天起，你来看炉。」你揭了东墙的「看丹炉」牌，守在他的炉边：火是他自己灌的灵力，药归你看；炉底下是地火，从石缝里透上来；首尾武，中间文，鼻子认糊味。清明替外公烧了纸。一晃五年，一层一式：灵草谷装睡的犰狳（定风），沂水东岸的鯥——头一块红木牌，肋骨断了一根，赢得难看（随风，六层）；器房老铁头的砧子上，鯥皮鯥翅膜做成一双「顺风溜」；寻人的青木牌，一只布鞋；七层卡了大半年（入隙）；第三年阿禾先筑了基，观主袖子里的丹；祁长松也筑了基。
recap.en: The dining hall said you stole spirit herbs from the garden to make pills; Zhou Heng opened the night-watch book: "The herb garden, not one plant short. The culls are the night watch's pay, written on the tag in the Hall of Errands… if you say he stole, bring the stolen goods." In private only one line: Sun Ergou's pill, "I looked. Two turns." The line went round — Shen Xiaoman has pills, good ones — and reached the pill house: Pill-master Min, thirty years at the furnace, sent for you and asked to see one; his lips stopped at the second ring: "Two turns. Better than what comes out of my furnace." He smelled it three times: "This pill didn't come out of a furnace. No fire in it." You said it came from a dead man's bag in the secret realm; he did not ask twice, only: "From tomorrow, you come and watch the furnace." You took the east wall's furnace-watch tag and kept his fire night after night: pine the fierce fire, oak the gentle, the nose to catch a batch turning. At Qingming you burned paper for Grandfather. Five years, a form a layer: the sham-sleeping Qiuyu in the Spirit-Herb Valley (stilling the wind); the Lu on the east bank of the Yi — a red tag, a rib broken, won ugly (going with the wind, layer six); on Old Ironhead's anvil in the forge house, Lu hide and wing-membrane became a pair of Tailwind Slippers; a green find-him tag, one cloth shoe; stuck most of a year at seven (entering the gap); in the third year A-He laid her Foundation first, on a pill from the abbot's sleeve; Qi Changsong laid his.

zh: 「这丹，不是炉里出来的。没有火气。」
en: "If you say he stole, bring the stolen goods."
"This pill didn't come out of a furnace. No fire in it."

story.zh:
这话到了内门饭堂里，便换了个讲法。一个大比时才四层的，一开春便是五层，还一包一包的丹送人——药园是他巡的。偷灵草炼丹，倒比死人的袋子说得通。

周衡在饭堂门口发灵石，听见了。他没有抬头，把巡夜簿翻开，一页一页往后翻，翻到末了，道：「药园，一株不少。残株是巡夜的工钱，执事堂的牌子上写着，一个月一篮，账上有。」他合上簿子，冲着那一桌：「要说他偷，拿赃来。」饭堂里没有人有赃。那一桌低下头吃饭了。

人散了，周衡却叫住小满，把账簿往胳膊底下一夹，低声道：「孙二狗那颗聚气丹，我看了。二转。」顿了一顿，「外门的份例，一纹。」他没再说什么，走了。往后小满月底照旧去执事堂交差，照旧领回一篮残株，周衡再没问过一个字；可每回把篮子推过来，他都要多看小满一眼。

周衡挡得住一个「偷」字，挡不住一屋子的嘴。第二天，那句话换了个说法：偷没偷不知道，沈小满手里有丹，好丹。这一句，比「偷」字要命——山上九层卡了十年八年的人，比丹多；比他高的人，也比丹多。这句话，传到了丹房。

沉鼎观的丹，都是丹房里出的。丹房在正殿西北角，一间矮屋，常年门窗紧闭，墙根熏得乌黑；屋里一口炉子，守炉的是内门的闵丹师——筑基圆满，在这口炉子跟前守了三十年，卡在结丹的门槛外也有十来年了。观里每月的份例聚气丹，每年大比那一颗筑基丹，都是他的手艺。上至执事，下至内门，谁的丹都出在他的炉里，没有人敢得罪他；逢年过节，丹房门口的礼盒堆到过膝，他一样也不看，爱收的收，不爱收的原样退回去，连送礼的人带盒子一起关在门外。他谁的面子也不给，三十年没人跟他红过脸。

第三天晌午，一个道童到药园来找小满：「闵丹师叫你去丹房。」

小满去了。他进门的时候，闵丹师正蹲在炉前，指尖游出一缕火灵力，一寸一寸地把炉灰拨开，背对着门，又瘦又驼，一件灰袍子烧出十几个洞，袍角上的洞最多。他没有回头，道：「把门关上。」小满关了门。屋里只有炉膛里一点暗红，药气又苦又重，呛得人眼睛发涩。

闵丹师拨完了灰，才站起来，在一张矮桌后头坐下，道：「听说你手里有丹。拿一颗我看看。」

小满站着没动。他心里把这个人过了一遍：观里每一颗一道纹的丹，都是这口炉子里出来的；拿一颗份例丹糊弄他，等于抱着人家的孩子给人家认。他爹说过，猎户不走没把握的路。他从怀里摸出一个油纸包，打开来，一颗青白透亮的丹，搁在了矮桌上。两道纹的——饭桶那个月吐的；九道的那一颗早在阿禾怀里，他身上也没有第二颗。

闵丹师没有伸手，先看。看了一会儿，才拿两根指头捏起来，凑到眼前，对着炉膛里那一点红，慢慢地转。他的嘴唇一动一动的，跟阿禾那天一样，是在数纹。数到第二道，停了。「二转。」他说，「这一颗，比我炉里的好。」他把丹凑到鼻子底下，闻了一闻，又闻了一闻，闭上眼睛，闻了第三回。

「这丹，」他睁开眼睛，「不是炉里出来的。」

小满道：「丹师怎么看出来的？」

闵丹师道：「没有火气。」他把丹搁回油纸上，「炉里出的丹，火气要在丹上留三年——转了几回火，便有几回火气，鼻子一闻就有数。这一颗，一点火气也没有。」他看着那颗丹，隔了一会儿，又道：「像是地里长出来的。」

小满没有作声。

闵丹师道：「哪儿来的？」

小满道：「秘境里。潭边一个死人，袋子里一只瓶。」他说得不快也不慢，跟他爹说「前山没有兔子」一个口气。

闵丹师看着他，看了很久。炉膛里「噼啪」响了一声。他没有说信，也没有说不信，只把那颗丹拿油纸原样包好，推了回来，道：「三十年，我这口炉子，一炉十颗，出两颗一纹的。」他没有再问第二遍。

小满把油纸包收进怀里，却没有走。他的眼睛落在那口炉子上，落了一会儿，道：「丹师，十颗只出两颗，另外八颗呢？」

闵丹师抬起眼皮。屋里很久没有人问过他这个了。「火不对。」他道，「武火过了头，药焦；文火不够，药生。」

「怎么知道过了头？」

「靠鼻子闻。」

「闻？」小满道，「我爹打猎，闻得出兔子刚过去还是过去半天了。药也是这样？」

闵丹师没有答，抬起一根手指，指尖凝出一丝火灵力，朝炉口送了进去，炉膛里的火便应声跳了一跳。「药下去，每一刻味儿都不同。」他道，「先是苦，苦里透甜，甜里冒一丝焦——那一丝，只有半口气的工夫。早一口，药没熟；晚一口，一炉全废。」他说着说着，声音低了下去，像是说给炉子听的，「来过十几个，鼻子都差在这半口气上。」

小满又问：「那这颗丹没有火气，是因为它没进过炉？没进炉，纹是哪儿来的？」

闵丹师指尖那一缕火灵力停在半空。他把这个问题在嘴里嚼了很久，道：「我不知道。」隔了一会儿，又道：「三十年了，头一回有人问到我答不上的。」

就在闵丹师出神的当口，炉里的药气变了，多出了一丝焦。他的神识全在火上，没有觉出来。小满耸了耸他那只狗鼻子，小声道：「丹师，这个……是不是就是丹焦的味儿？」

闵丹师猛地回头，指尖一收，火势立刻退了半分，那一炉药在炉里翻了个身，稳住了。他没有马上说话，把小满从头到脚打量了两眼，道：「你叫什么？沈小狗？」

一缕汗水顺着小满的太阳穴淌了下来。「回丹师，」他道，「我叫沈小满。」

「小满。」闵丹师把这两个字念了一遍，「小成而知满，不贪，好名字。」他顿了一顿，「那块牌子挂了三年，我叫进来的人，没有一个闻得出。你头一回进这屋，闻出来了；问的，也都是该问的。这是块炼丹的料。火我自己灌，旁人替不了；药，往后归你看。明天去执事堂，把牌子揭了，来报到。」

小满道：「……我不会。」闵丹师道：「不会，学。鼻子是学不来的，别的都学得来。」

他从矮桌底下抽出一册手抄的薄本，蓝布面，边角磨得起毛，往小满怀里一扔。封面写着两个字：《金丹》，底下一行小字：抱朴子内篇卷四。「葛洪写的，天底下炼丹的人，头一本都是它。」闵丹师道，「丹怎么分转，怎么封泥，怎么起火，开炉前要斋戒，里头都有。你抄三遍，一个字不许错。书上说的是理，火你得自己闻。看不懂的圈出来，明天问。」

小满道：「是。」

他出了丹房，走了十几步，才觉出后背上一层汗。那个人没有留他的丹，没有问他第二遍，也没有去执事房；他自己倒是问了一堆，问到最后，把一块牌子问到了手里。可他心里明白，这座山上，往后多了一双眼睛看着他——那双眼睛，比周衡的更会看，而且往后天天看。只是这一回，看他的人是想要他留下来。

丹房的门关上了，内门饭堂里那句话便慢慢地没了声。有人问起，便有人答：「闵丹师看过了。」看过了怎么样，没人知道；过了半个月，没人再提了。

第二天他去执事堂，把东墙上「丹房 · 看丹炉」那块乌木牌揭了下来。邓执事抬眼看了看，道：「这块，三年没人揭了。」小满去执事房领差，周衡在账上记了一笔：看炉，记功。

看炉看的是药，不是火。火是闵丹师自己的：开炉那几天，他站在炉口上头，两只手悬着，一口灵力接一口灵力地往里灌，眼睛也不眨。小满的活在炉子旁边：看药，闻药，碾药，递东西。头一夜闵丹师什么也没教，只往炉边一指：「你就坐这儿。」小满便坐了一夜，看那一点暗红。看着看着，他觉出不对：炉底下没有柴，没有炭，连风箱也没有。炉膛里那点红，是从底下一道石缝里透上来的，他伸手一探，石缝是烫的。

第二夜，闵丹师总算开了口。「火有四样。」他伸出四根手指，一根一根地掰，「凡火，柴炭糠壳，烧饭取暖的火，炼不出丹，只好煨药。地火，地底下的火，老坑里一眼，千年不灭，稳，不躁；观里这口炉子，就坐在上头，三百年了。可地火是死的，烧不成丹；得丹师把自己的灵力灌进去，引着它，火才活，灌多灌少，便是文武。丹火，」他停了停，「是人自己身上的火，结了丹的人才有，一口气吐出来，比地火还纯。」小满问：「第四样呢？」闵丹师看了他一眼，好一会儿才道：「真火。比如太上老君的三昧真火。」

第三夜，炉里有一炉药，到了后半夜，闵丹师忽然道：「你闻闻看。」小满闻了，药气里多了一丝焦，像锅巴刚要糊的那一下。闵丹师把炉门关了一半，道：「记住这个味儿。晚一口气，一炉都是药引。」顿了一顿，又道：「《参同契》上有一句：首尾武，中间文。开头要猛，叫药醒；中间要缓，叫药熟；收尾再猛，把药锁住。什么时候换，鼻子告诉你，书上不告诉你。」他看着药，闵丹师守着火。

第七天，闵丹师开了一炉聚气丹。药斗一字排开，他一样一样报给小满听，像报名册：「黄精为君，黄芪、当归为臣，人参须为使，灵石末为引。一君二臣一使，缺一味，药不合。」小满蹲在药斗边上，嘴里没出声，心里一样一样地对：黄精，他喂过；黄芪，当归，他也喂过，只是分开喂的；灵石，喂过；单单没有人参。他想起饭桶那张时吐时不吐的嘴，一下子明白了：它不是脾气坏，是方子缺了一味。

那天夜里，他从药园的篮子里倒出两根紫玉参的断须，搭着黄精、黄芪、当归，连同一块灵石，一股脑喂了进去。「咯嘣」，「咯嘣」，「咔哒」——吐出来的聚气丹，青白透亮，纹是两道。他对着窗缝里漏进来的月光看了很久，把它收进了那只贴身的油纸包。
story.en:
In the inner court's dining hall the talk took another shape. Layer four at the contest, layer five come spring, and packet after packet of pills to give away — and he was the one who patrolled the herb garden. Stealing spirit herbs to make pills made better sense than a dead man's bag.

Zhou Heng was handing out spirit stones at the dining-hall door, and heard. He did not look up; he opened the night-watch book and turned the pages one by one to the end, and said: "The herb garden: not one plant short. The culls are the night watch's pay — it is written on the tag in the Hall of Errands, one basket a month, and it is in the ledger." He shut the book and faced that table: "If you say he stole, bring the stolen goods." Nobody in the hall had any. That table bent over its bowls.

When the hall emptied, Zhou Heng called Xiaoman back, tucked the ledger under his arm and said, low: "Sun Ergou's qi pill — I looked. Two turns." A pause. "The outer court's allowance is one ring." He said nothing more and left. After that Xiaoman went to the Hall of Errands at every month's end as before to hand in the job, and came away with a basket of culls as before, and Zhou Heng never asked another word; but each time he pushed the basket across, he looked at Xiaoman a moment longer.

Zhou Heng could stop the word "theft"; he could not stop a roomful of mouths. The next day the line had changed its shape: theft or no theft, who knew — Shen Xiaoman had pills, good pills. That was deadlier than "theft" — on this mountain there were more people stuck at layer nine for eight or ten years than there were pills; and more people stronger than him than there were pills, too. The line reached the pill house.

Every pill of Chending Temple came out of the pill house: a low room at the north-west corner of the main hall, its door and windows kept shut the year round, the foot of its walls smoked black; inside, one furnace, and keeping it, Pill-master Min of the inner court — Foundation at Consummation, thirty years at this one furnace. The ration qi pills each month and the one Foundation pill at each year's contest were all his work.

At noon on the third day a temple boy came to the herb garden for Xiaoman: "Pill-master Min wants you at the pill house."

Xiaoman went. When he came in, Pill-master Min was squatting before the furnace raking the ash with an iron poker, his back to the door — thin, stooped, in a grey robe burnt through in a dozen places, most of them at the hem. He didn't turn round. "Shut the door behind you." Xiaoman shut it. The only light in the room was a dull red in the furnace mouth; the drug smell was bitter and heavy, and it stung the eyes.

Only when the ash was raked did Pill-master Min stand up and sit down behind a low table. "I hear you have pills. Let me see one."

Xiaoman didn't move. He went over the man in his head: every one-ring pill in this temple had come out of that furnace; to fob him off with a ration pill was to hold a man's own child up for him to recognise. His father used to say a hunter doesn't take a path he isn't sure of. He took an oilpaper packet from inside his coat, opened it, and set a pill, blue-white and clear, on the low table. A two-ring one — the Rice Tub's from that month; the nine was long since in A-He's jacket, and he had no second.

Pill-master Min did not reach for it; he looked first. After a while he picked it up in two fingers, brought it close to his eyes and turned it slowly against the one red point in the furnace. His lips moved, as A-He's had that day — counting rings. At the second he stopped. "Two turns," he said. "This one is better than what comes out of my furnace." He put the pill under his nose, smelled it once, smelled it again, shut his eyes and smelled it a third time.

"This pill," he said, opening his eyes, "didn't come out of a furnace."

Xiaoman said: "How can the master tell?"

"No fire in it," said Pill-master Min. He set the pill back on the paper. "A furnace pill keeps its fire for three years — as many turns in the fire, that many fires to smell; one sniff tells you. This one has none at all." He looked at the pill a while longer, and added: "As if it grew out of the ground."

Xiaoman said nothing.

Pill-master Min said: "Where did it come from?"

Xiaoman said: "In the secret realm. A dead man by the pool, a bottle in his bag." He said it neither fast nor slow, in the voice his father used for "no hares on the front hill".

Pill-master Min looked at him for a long time. Something cracked in the furnace. He did not say he believed it and did not say he didn't; he only wrapped the pill back in its oilpaper as it had been and pushed it across: "Thirty years, my furnace: ten to a batch, two with one ring." He did not ask a second time.

Xiaoman tucked the packet into his jacket and thanked him. At the door, Pill-master Min spoke behind him: "Shen Xiaoman." Xiaoman stopped. "From tomorrow," said Pill-master Min, "you come and watch the furnace."

"…Watch the furnace?" said Xiaoman. "On the east wall of the Hall of Errands there's a tag for watching the furnace," said Pill-master Min. "Take it down, then come."

"Yes," said Xiaoman.

He was a dozen steps out of the pill house before he felt the sweat on his back. The man had not kept his pill, had not asked twice, had not gone to the steward's office. But he knew that from now on there was one more pair of eyes on this mountain watching him — eyes that saw better than Zhou Heng's — and from now on they would watch every day.

With the pill-house door shut, the line in the inner court's dining hall slowly lost its voice. If someone asked, someone answered: "Pill-master Min has looked." Looked and found what, nobody knew; half a month on, no one spoke of it.

Next day he went to the Hall of Errands and took the ebony tag *Pill house · Watch the furnace* off the east wall. Steward Deng looked up: "Nobody has taken that one in three years." Xiaoman went to the steward's office for the job, and Zhou Heng wrote a line in the ledger: furnace watch, merit.

Watching the furnace meant watching the herbs, not the fire. The fire was Pill-master Min's own: in the days a batch was going he stood over the furnace mouth, both hands held above it, pouring in his spirit power breath after breath, never blinking. Xiaoman's work was beside the furnace: watching the herbs, smelling them, grinding them, handing things over. The first night Pill-master Min taught nothing; he pointed at the furnace: "You sit here." Xiaoman sat the night through, watching the one dull red point. As he watched, something seemed wrong: under the furnace there was no wood, no charcoal, not even a bellows. The red in the firebox came up through a crack in the stone beneath; he put out a hand, and the crack was hot.

The second night Pill-master Min spoke at last. "Fire comes in four kinds." He held up four fingers and bent them down one by one. "Common fire — wood, charcoal, chaff, husks; the fire you cook by and warm yourself at. It won't make a pill; it's good for stewing herbs. Earth fire — the fire under the ground; one vent in an old pit burns a thousand years and never goes out, steady, never rash. This temple's furnace sits right on one, and has for three hundred years. But earth fire is dead and won't make a pill by itself; the pill-master has to pour his own spirit power in and lead it, and then the fire lives — how much he pours is fierce or gentle. Pill fire," he paused, "is the fire in a man himself. Only one who has formed his Core has it; one breath of it is purer than earth fire." Xiaoman asked: "And the fourth?" Pill-master Min looked at him, and only after a good while said: "True fire. The Samadhi True Fire of Lord Laozi, say."

The third night there was a batch in the furnace, and deep in the night Pill-master Min said suddenly: "Smell it — go on." Xiaoman smelled: in the herb-reek a thread of scorch, like rice crust the instant before it burns. Pill-master Min half-closed the furnace door. "Remember that smell. One breath late and the whole batch is for grinding." After a moment he went on: "The *Cantong Qi* has a line: fierce at head and tail, gentle in the middle. Fierce at the start, to wake the herbs; slow in the middle, to cook them; fierce again at the close, to lock them in. When to change, your nose tells you; the book doesn't." Xiaoman watched the herbs; Pill-master Min kept the fire.

On the seventh day Pill-master Min opened a batch of qi pills. The herb drawers stood in a row, and he named them for Xiaoman one by one, like reading out a register: "Solomon's seal is the sovereign; milkvetch and angelica the ministers; ginseng whiskers the envoy; spirit-stone dust the guide. One sovereign, two ministers, one envoy — lack one and the herbs won't agree." Xiaoman squatted by the drawers, saying nothing aloud, checking them off in his head: Solomon's seal, he had fed it; milkvetch and angelica, he had fed those too, only separately; spirit stones, fed; ginseng alone, never. He thought of the Rice Tub's mouth, that gave a pill one time and not the next, and suddenly understood: it wasn't temper. The recipe was short one herb.

That night he tipped two broken whiskers of purple-jade ginseng out of the herb-garden basket and fed them in with Solomon's seal, milkvetch and angelica, and a spirit stone besides, all at once. *Crunch*, *crunch*, *click* — the qi pill it spat out was blue-white and clear, with two rings. He looked at it a long time in the moonlight leaking through the crack of the window, and put it away in the oilpaper packet he kept next to his skin.

exits.means: the spring: burns paper for his grandfather facing Mengshan; A-He's strip of rice by the herb-garden wall, fed with her own qi (they drink more than the herbs); she swallows her nine-ring pill there — layer seven, short of what it should give, the rice gone nearly black-green overnight

story.zh:
清明那天，他在后山寻了一块向着蒙山的石头，替外公烧了一沓黄纸——外公的坟在镇上，他去不了。他念着他娘教的口诀，念到「五居中央」，纸烧完了，灰飞起来，打着旋儿往山下去。

那天傍晚，他去药园东角寻阿禾。她白天管药园，他夜里巡园，两个人一天总要碰上两回。她在东角墙根底下拔了一溜杂草，空出巴掌宽的一条地，没跟谁说。开春她启了竹筒上的蜡，倒出那三粒黑谷——秘境黑地里抠来的，有人种过地的老谷，黑得发亮，硬得像石子——埋了下去，出了三棵芽，一棵一棵地黄。她便夜夜掐着兰花诀，掌心朝下，隔着一寸，拿自己的灵力喂它们。一园子的药草，她喂惯了，喂完一畦，额头上见一层汗；这三棵苗，她要喂到后半夜，脸白得跟窗户纸一样。喂了二十来夜，那三棵苗的叶尖，终于不再往下黄了，嫩生生地挺了起来。

小满蹲在她旁边看了一会儿，道：「它们喝你的灵力。」

阿禾道：「喝得比一园子药草还多。」她把手收回来，在衣襟上擦了擦，「老谷，不知饿了多少年了。」

那颗九道纹的聚气丹，她一直揣着。那天夜里，她蹲在地头把它吞了，一只手按着土，坐到天亮。天亮的时候，她是练气七层了。这样一颗丹该冲多远，她在藏经阁里查过，心里有数——差了一截。墙根底下那三棵苗，一夜之间，绿得发黑。
story.en:
On Qingming he found a rock on the back hill facing Mengshan and burned a stack of yellow paper for Grandfather — Grandfather's grave was in the town, and he could not go. He recited the formula his mother had taught him; as he reached "five in the middle", the paper burned out, and the ash flew up and spun away down the mountain.

That evening he went to find A-He at the east corner of the herb garden. She kept the garden by day and he patrolled it by night, so the two of them ran into each other twice a day at least. Along the foot of the east wall she had pulled a strip of weeds and cleared a palm's width of ground, and told nobody. In spring she broke the wax on her bamboo tube, shook out the rice seed and sowed it; twenty-odd shoots came up, and one by one they yellowed. So every night she held the orchid seal, palm down an inch above the soil, and fed them with her own qi. The herbs of a whole garden she was used to feeding — a bed done, and a film of sweat on her brow; these twenty-odd stalks she had to feed till past midnight, and her face went as white as window paper. The rice stopped yellowing.

Xiaoman squatted beside her and watched a while, and said: "They're drinking your qi."

"More than a whole garden of herbs," said A-He. She took her hand back and wiped it on her jacket. "Grown on hillside fields. They're used to going hungry."

The nine-ring qi pill she had kept on her all along. That night she squatted at the head of the strip and swallowed it, one hand pressed to the soil, and sat till dawn. At dawn she was at Qi Refining layer seven. How far a pill like that ought to carry you she had looked up in the scripture library, and she knew — it had come up short. Along the foot of the wall, in a single night, the twenty-odd stalks had gone a green so deep it was nearly black.

label.en: The dog days · Five years go by

exits.means: the hot months: nights on the herb-garden wall with A-He and Sun Ergou — then five years run on the 执事堂's tags, a mission and a 巽四 form per layer (three to a tag; 阿禾 plans, 小满 fights, 孙二狗 takes the blows): year three the 犰狳 at 灵草谷 (the sleep is a sham; 定风 sees the first twitch, he wins hurt; the locusts are the real pest — 阿禾 has the turf burned); 瞿老's 随风 lesson (列子御风; 「打不透的，别打。等它漏气」); year four the 鯥 of 沂水东岸 — a red tag, a 六层 beast at 五层: 定风 at its shoulder, the 火柴 leaves a white mark, a rib cracked, he runs up the bank, 随风 through the 禹步 beside it, 入隙 at the fin root on the third glide; 六层 that night, from the fight, not a pill; the 器房 — a month on 老铁头's bellows, one night at the forge, 洗料·合形·刻纹, the 巽 lines cut straight (「……你师父是谁？」), the 顺风溜 (ten 丈 a glide downwind, nothing against the wind); year five the widow's green tag, a shoe brought back; 七层 and the stall, 入隙 (庖丁), 碾药 with 闵丹师; 祁长松 fails his first 筑基, lays it on the second, flies into the east-corner cypress; A-He, fifteen, lays her Foundation on the abbot's pill, hidden, and teases him with interest

story.zh:
伏天里最热的那几夜，药园巡完了，三个人常坐在药园的矮墙上乘凉：小满，阿禾，孙二狗。

小满问：「你想叫什么？」孙二狗想了半天，道：「……还叫二狗吧。我娘叫惯了。」

小满没笑。阿禾也没笑。墙底下的小狰翻了个身，打了个响鼻。

一晃，便是五年。

沈小满这五年，大抵一年一层。说书的先讲头三年：五层，六层，七层。秘境里那一撮土长成的厚地，吸一口，存一口；饭桶一个月吐给他一两颗聚气丹，偶尔一颗三道四道的，他收起来，不吃；一层吃到半缸，他便停了，余下的半缸，夜里自己一口一口吸满。他娘讲他这个名字：满了就要溢，饱了一点，还知道饿。

《吐纳经》上那一口气，一层换一副样子。五层，吸一口，缸里听得见响，像往空瓮里倒水；六层，水面高了，响没了，吐一口比吸一口长出一半来；七层，气往脚底下沉——他爹当年在雪地里说的那一句，他到这时候才知道沉到哪里：沉到脚跟。

灵石呢，起先是执事堂西墙上挣的。

年三入了秋，他揭了头一块牌：蒙山北灵草谷，夜里有妖，六层，未开灵智，吃灵草，伤人，每人二十块灵石。邓执事看了看牌，又看了看他：「五层了？」小满道：「五层了。」邓执事道：「妖是六层的，比你高一层。一个人不许去。差事牌，三个人起。」小满回头，身后站着两个人：一个是跟来看热闹的孙二狗，一层；一个是阿禾，手里还提着药园的小锄头。阿禾道：「我去。我倒想瞧瞧，是什么妖怪喜欢吃灵草。」邓执事看了看她，没说什么，便在簿子上写了三个名字。

灵草谷在蒙山北，走大半天，谷里的田全种着观里要的灵草，几户药农看着，一年交一回货。妖是真有的：入夜便有一样东西蹲在田埂上，兔子大小，鸟嘴，一双猫头鹰的圆眼，拖一条蛇尾巴，人一走近，它便倒下装死；天一亮，田里的灵草少一片。谷里人拿锄头打着过它，它翻个身又跑了，灵草照旧少；守夜的汉子已经伤了两个，一个小腿给啄穿了，一个肩膀给蛇尾巴抽折了。管谷的老药农把一根锄头柄拿给他们看：柄上一道豁口，上下对穿，断茬齐得像剪刀铰过的。小满拿手指头比了比那道豁口的宽窄，没有作声。兔子大小的东西，嘴张不到这么开；张得到这么开的东西，不会给锄头打跑。

三个人在田埂上蹲了一夜。三更过后，那东西果然来了，从灵草垄里一蹦一蹦地出来，一见人影便躺倒，肚皮朝天，连尾巴都不动一动。孙二狗举着灯笼，弯腰看了半天，小声道：「它、它睡着了。」小满搭箭要射，阿禾按住了他的弓：「等等。」

她蹲下去，没看那只妖的肚皮，看的是它身上的灵力。那团灵力浊黄里透着青，缩得紧紧的，不像睡着的东西，倒像一个把拳头攥在背后的人。「六层，木的底子。」她低声道，「《山海经》{典=shanhai-qiuyu}里有它。[犰狳]{注=qiuyu}，见人则眠。」小满的手指在弦上紧了一紧：他自己是五层。

那只犰狳的眼皮动了。

它没有起身，是翻了个身，四脚落地，一下便蹿到了孙二狗跟前。孙二狗还弯着腰，举着灯笼，嘴张着：「它、它——」鸟嘴「咔」地合在灯笼上，灯笼碎成了三片，灯油泼了一地，火苗顺着油窜上了他的袖口。他尖叫一声，一屁股坐在田埂上，坐在那条蛇尾巴够得着的地方。

阿禾右手飞快地掐了一个兰花诀，朝田埂上一指，灵力隔空往地里一沉，地皮底下「嗖」地窜出三根青藤，两根缠住后腿，一根勒上了腰，把它的后半截钉在原地，只许它拧着身子，嘴和尾巴够得着多远，便咬多远。它一挣，藤便「啪」地断了一根。「这妖浑身蛮力，」阿禾眉头一紧，右手的诀没有松，「我没法困住它太久！」左手却已经掐了一个诀，隔着三丈远，朝孙二狗的袖口虚虚一按：一缕青色的灵力淌过去，那团火苗伏下去，灭了，袖口底下烫红的皮肉，一点一点退了红。「别动！」她喊，「你一动，我两头顾不上！」

小满没有看她，他的脚早动了。他心里有九格——瞿老河洛剑诀的头一课，先有脚，后有剑——这时他站进了巽位，左脚落在东南那一格，剑还没出，人先斜出了半格，火柴的剑尖垂在地上，擦着泥：巽卦底下一道是断的，软的在底下。五层的火柴，灌足了灵力，剑刃上浮着一层油光。他爹说过，风要歇一口气。他等着。

他踩的每一格，都在它够得着的那一圈的边上；藤每断一根，那一圈便大一尺。鸟嘴一口撕在他方才站的那一格里，「咔」，上下喙一合，咬了个空。他踏到下一格。它再咬他的肋下，他再踏一格；一口接着一口——它比他快，比他快得多，可每一口咬下去之前，眼珠子都要先动那么一动；一口比一口狠，一口比一口短。蛇尾巴却躲不过，一鞭抽在他小腿上，像给人拿鞭子抽了一下，裤腿湿了。又是两鞭，三道棱子一道一道肿起来。

偏在这时候，孙二狗动了。他看见火灭了，爬起来要跑，慌不择路，一头撞进了小满那一格里。小满剑尖一偏，侧身用左肩把他扛开，这一扛，慢了半步，那条蛇尾巴「啪」地横扫过来，把孙二狗抽得离了地，飞出三丈远，摔进灵草垄里，一声没吭。阿禾那边又「啪」地断了一根藤。「小满，」她的声音绷得紧紧的，「快，我撑不了多久。」

她松开右手半根指头，左手朝孙二狗那边一翻：青色的灵力顺着垄沟淌过去，孙二狗脚踝上那一大块青紫，一点一点退了下去，他睁开眼睛，哼了一声。阿禾额上见了一层细汗，呼吸急了些，眼睛一直没离开那几根藤。

就在这时，最后一根藤，「啪」地断了。

它没了束缚，整个身子压了过来，不再一口一口地咬，是撞——鸟嘴、蛇尾、四只爪子一齐上。小满的九格一下子乱了：往右退，是孙二狗躺着的那一片，他还没爬起来；往左退，是灵草垄的深沟，退下去，孙二狗便整个落在它爪子底下。进，是它的嘴；退，是孙二狗的命。他左右都是死路，剑尖在身前划了一个又一个半圆，只守，不敢攻，鸟嘴贴着他的脖子过去，削掉了一缕头发，蛇尾「啪」地抽在他腰上，抽得他连退三格，剑险些脱手。

「小满，撑住！」阿禾喊。她撤了缠藤的那一诀，右手另掐一诀，朝那只犰狳脚底下一指，那里三尺的地皮「噗噗」地拱开，一大片荆棘窜了出来，枝条上全是倒钩，叶片边缘一圈细细的锯齿；荆棘一丛挤着一丛，连个下脚的缝都没有。它一脚下去，倒钩扎进肉里，一动，锯齿便在腿上拉出一道血口。一株灵草也没碰着。那只犰狳的动作忽然慢了：爪子抬起来，落下去，每挪一步，都要先把腿从荆棘里拔出来；它平日见人就躺，这一回，连躺都躺不下去——一躺，满身是刺。

小满等的就是这半拍。他左手掐了个剑诀，并指从剑根往剑尖一抹，从丹田里抽出细细一缕金系的灵力，顺着手臂灌进火柴。暗红的剑身上镀上了一层白森森的光，像冬夜里结在铜壶上的霜，剑刃一下子薄了，也利了。他五门里最弱的一门，也就够这么一回。

他脚尖在孙二狗身边的田埂上一点，整个人拔地而起，越过了那只犰狳的头顶——荆棘丛里它挪不动，只能仰起脖子，眼睁睁看着一个人影从月亮底下压下来。镀了金的火柴剑尖朝下，一道白光，从它后颈扎了进去，扎到了底。它连一声都没叫完，在剑上抽了两下，不动了。他人还在半空里，嘴上没闲着：「还好我的金能克它。」

小满落了下来，落在阿禾那一大片荆棘里。阿禾撤法术的手，和他落地是同一个眨眼，荆棘「呼」地缩了回去，还是晚了那么一瞬。

他摔了个四脚朝天，倒钩勾住了袖子，锯齿在手背和脸上拉出几道口子，倒钩的尖刺扎了一手。荆棘退得干干净净，他一骨碌爬起来，顶着满脸的血口子，朝阿禾看了一眼，举起手，咧着嘴：「好厉害的法术！」他扮了个鬼脸，「以后可不敢惹你生气了。」

阿禾喘着气，抬头看了他一眼：「记住了就好。」她走上前来，一把抓过他的手腕，另一只手掐了个诀，掌心里透出一层青色的灵力，凉丝丝的，像雨后的草叶子贴在皮上。他手上脸上那几道血口子一道一道收了皮，血珠凝住了，疼也一点一点退了；小腿上的鞭痕，腰上的青紫，淡下去一层。「别动，」她板着脸，「还有几根刺在肉里，一会儿给你拔。」小满老老实实坐着，再不敢扮鬼脸。

谷里人举着火把围上来的时候，小满坐在田埂上，手上脸上荆棘划的口子刚收了皮，裤腿割开，小腿上三道鞭痕还肿着，底下一个深深的喙印，阿禾也只给他止了血——不知什么时候啄着的，他自己都没觉得；腰上还有一大块青紫。他摸出一颗回春丹吞了，道：「它不睡。」阿禾蹲下去看了看他的腿，道：「书上说见人则眠。书上没说眠是装的。」她把这一句记进了小本子。

天亮，谷里人送了两吊钱、一篮子鸡蛋。老药农还拿刀把那只犰狳剥了，剥出三样东西来：一对鸱鸟的圆眼珠，浑圆，黄澄澄的，夜里对着火把还亮；一副鸟喙，边口锋利得像剪刀；还有一段带斑的蛇尾皮，软而韧。老药农道：「眼珠，药铺肯收，能做夜视的药引。喙和皮，各位自己分。」三个人分了：眼珠归小满，他杀的；喙归阿禾，她要拿回去，对着《山海经》再记一笔；蛇尾皮归孙二狗，他替大家挨了一尾巴，该得一样。孙二狗抱着那段蛇皮，半天说不出话来。回到观里，邓执事把牌子翻过来，背面一个「讫」字，数出六十块灵石，三个人一人二十块。阿禾接过自己那一份，数也没数，掏出小本子记了一笔。小满道：「记的什么？」阿禾道：「鸡蛋。十二个。」顿了一顿，「利息另算。」

说书的在这里插一句：这一趟，阿禾救的是三个人的命，小满赢的是一场装睡的对决，赢得不好看。往后五年，大抵都是这个样子——她看地，他看人；她想法子，他出手；挨打的，是孙二狗。

瞿老一个月两回，在崖顶上拿扫帚把教他巽四的剑，他拿那口火柴跟着学。瞿老教剑不多话，一层一式，一式一句。五年里，剑柄上缠的布，换了三回。

年四开春，教的是随风。那天崖顶上起风，瞿老站在巽那一格上，手里捏着一片叶子，松开，叶子飞起来，他的扫帚把便跟着那片叶子走，叶子往东，扫帚把往东，叶子打一个旋，扫帚把打一个旋，不快不慢，像一个人牵着一条狗。「你定住了，看得见风起来。」瞿老道，「看见了，别顶。顶是艮，你不是山。跟着它走半截，它的劲就卸了一半；剩下的一半，才是你的。」他念了一句书：「《庄子》{典=zhuangzi-liezi}里说，『列子御风而行，泠然善也』——列子踩着风走路，走得真轻快。底下还有一句：『犹有所待者也』。他还得等风。」他把扫帚靠回墙角，「这门剑诀，借的是风。借风的人，走得再轻，也得有风。祖师留下的只有半卷，到结丹为止；结丹往上，要的是不借东西的本事，这半卷里没有。你先借着。」临走，他又添了一句，像是顺口：「打不透的，别打。等它漏气。」

随风，他是在沂水东岸学会的。

那年入秋，西墙上挂出一块红木牌：「沂水东岸，夜里有牛首之怪上岸，拖走耕牛三头。灵石四块。」挂牌的是沂水边上一个穷村的里正，字是县里的书办代写的。老油子看了一眼，走了——四块灵石，三头牛，不知道是什么东西，不值。它挂了七天。第八天早上，小满把它揭了下来。邓执事道：「五层揭红牌？」小满道：「五层揭得。」邓执事看了他一会儿，在簿子上写了三个名字。

他看那块牌，看的不是字，是脚印。三头牛，没写见血——牛那么大的东西，叫什么咬死了，田埂上总要有血；没有血，便是没咬死，是活活拖走的；拖走的，不是往山里拖，是往水里拖。什么东西拖得动一头牛？他想了一夜，没想出来。想不出来，便照他爹的法子：先看风，后看鹿；看不见鹿，先把人摆好。

三个人到了沂水东岸，天已经黑了。里正把他们领到河滩上。滩上牛蹄印乱七八糟，蹄印中间，有一道拖痕，两尺宽，从牛圈一直拖进水里，拖痕两边，一边一行不深不浅的爪印，爪印当中是一道弯弯曲曲的沟，像一条粗绳在泥上拖过。阿禾蹲下去看了那道沟，道：「蛇尾巴。」又看了看爪印，道：「四条腿，蹄子。」她翻开小本子，翻到后头，念道：「《山海经》{典=shanhai-lu}南山经柢山：『有鱼焉，其状如牛，陵居，蛇尾有翼，其羽在魼下，其音如留牛，其名曰鯥，冬死而夏生。』」小满道：「鱼？」阿禾道：「[鯥]{注=lu}，是鱼，住在岸上，样子像牛，蛇尾巴，翅膀长在肋下。冬死夏生——它入冬要睡死过去，睡之前得吃饱。」她合上本子，「这会儿正是它最饿的时候。」

小满问：「多大？」阿禾道：「书上没写。拖得动牛。」里正要带人去守牛圈，小满摆摆手，叫全村的人都回屋，门闩上，火灭了。孙二狗把背上那块松木板卸下来——是他自己在柴房后头刨的，一人多高，钉了三道铁箍——往拖痕的口子上一戳，人站在板子后头，火把插在板子边上，照得他那张脸又白又亮。阿禾站在他身后两步，右手虚虚地掐着诀，指尖朝着滩上的泥。小满没站在明处，往下风头退了二十步，蹲进一丛芦苇里，火柴横在膝盖上。

这是一年里他们揭的第七块牌，不用谁吩咐谁。

月亮上来的时候，水响了。

那东西从水里上来，先露出来的是一颗牛头，两只角，一双牛眼睛在火把底下发绿；跟着上来的身子也是牛的，一身青黑的皮，油光光的，像鱼；身后拖着一条蛇尾巴，比它的身子还长，在滩上扫来扫去。它比牛小一圈，上了岸便不停，低着头，直冲着火把来——它眼里只有那一团亮，和亮底下那块板子。

孙二狗两只脚往泥里一插，膝盖一弯，屁股往下一坐。这是褚先生在讲堂上教过、外门人人都学过、却没几个人当回事的一路土行桩功，叫「山根桩」；孙二狗练了两年，别的都没练成，就练成了这一样：一站下去，脚底下像生了根。「咚」的一声，牛头撞在板子上，板子往后滑了三尺，在泥里犁出两道沟——停住了。孙二狗还站着，脸叫板子挤得歪到一边，嘴里喊着：「我是山……我是山……」

它退了一步，再撞，板子没退；那条蛇尾巴却从板子边上绕了过来，「呼」地扫向孙二狗的脚脖子。

阿禾右手一掐兰花诀，朝那条扫过来的尾巴一指。滩上「噗」地拱出一丛荆棘，倒钩朝外，尾巴扫进去，挂了一尾巴的刺；荆棘顺着尾巴往上爬，爬上它的后腿，一圈一圈勒紧了。它疼得一挣，挣不开，牛头抵着板子，后腿叫荆棘钉在滩上，进不得，退不得。

它肋下的皮张开了——是两片翅膀，薄得像蝙蝠的，一张开，有一张席子大。它要飞，要连着荆棘把自己拔出去。翅膀张开之前，它得吸一口气，吸气的时候，翅膀根上那块皮翻开来，翻开一霎，露出底下粉红的肉，像鱼的鳃。

小满在芦苇里等的就是这一霎。他扣在指间的那口短飞剑，诀一掐，放了出去，一道白光贴着滩上的泥飞过去，从那块粉红的肉里钻了进去。

它叫了一声，像牛叫，又拖着一个尾音，像人在水底下喊，翅膀张了一半，塌了下去。它挣了几下，不挣了，侧着身子躺在荆棘里，一只牛眼睛朝着天。

孙二狗这才从板子后头出来。他两条腿僵得打不了弯，一步一步挪过来，挪到小满身边，扑通坐下，看着自己的两只手——掌心叫板子边上的铁箍磨掉了两块皮，血糊糊的。阿禾蹲下去，搭了搭他的腕子，一缕灵力顺着腕子往下走了一遍，道：「骨头没事。」阿禾左手掐诀，一缕青光从指尖涌出，敷到伤口，立时便恢复了大半。孙二狗看着手心，咧着嘴笑：「沈师兄，我、我站住了。」小满道：「站住了。它撞了你两回。」孙二狗道：「三回。」他伸出三根指头，「头一回你没看见，我数着呢。」

天亮了，里正带着全村的人下到河滩上，把它从荆棘里拖出来，比牛小一圈，青黑的皮在日头底下泛着蓝。全村的人吃了三天肉，肉是鱼味的，不腥。里正送了一篮鸡蛋，一坛酒。小满要了两样东西：它肋下那两片翅膀的膜，薄，韧，对着日头看，透亮，兜得住风；它背上那张皮，厚得出奇，里正拿刀剥了半天，刀刃卷了三回。皮和膜他拿盐揉了，卷起来，背回了山。

回到泗水边上，天已经擦黑了。孙二狗坐了半夜桩，两条腿还是僵的，下不得台阶，阿禾架着他先上去；小满蹲在渡口底下的浅水里，把那张皮再漂一遍——盐没揉透，腥气熏人，背进西廊，四个人一屋，要挨骂的。

河水忽然不响了。

不是风停了，是水停了。浅水里那几根水草，本来顺着水一摆一摆，这时候直直地立着，像插在冰里。岸上的秋虫，方才还叫成一片，一下子全哑了。月亮照在水面上，水面平得像一块镜子，一丝纹也不起。小满胸口的木牌，冰了一下，冰得他手一缩，那张皮掉进了水里。

「鱼皮。」身后有人道，「好东西。」

那嗓子又干又深，像有人趴在一口老井口上往底下喊。小满没回头，后脖颈子上的汗毛一根一根立了起来。

他抄起搁在石头上的火柴，没回头，剑顺着河面上的风往后一送。白衣人站在渡口的石阶上，月光落在他那一身白上，白得发青；一只手背在身后，没动。剑尖到了他袖口跟前半尺，停住了，像扎在一口井的水面上，再进不去半分。小满的眼睛一下子睁圆了，嘴张着，一口气卡在嗓子眼里——他这一剑，灌足了灵力，到了这人跟前，连袖子都碰不着。

那人笑了。笑声不高，干干的，一声一声，像从井底下慢慢地往上冒，冒到井口，散不开，又沉回去。剑自己弹了回来，震得小满虎口一麻，裂了。

小满没出第二剑。他往后一退，是禹步，左脚先出，右脚绕过去——那人已经站在他身后了。他没看见那人迈步。一股凉气从他尾巴骨一路爬上后脑勺。

他把怀里那道遁符压进掌心，掐了个诀——金光一闪，他已经落在三丈外的浅水里。他一回头，脸上的血一下子退得干干净净：那一身白，就在他跟前，跟方才一般远，一般近，衣角上连一滴水都没沾。

「三丈。」那人道，又笑了一声，「好符。」

一根指头点在他胸口上，很轻。

小满整个人往后一折，躺进了水里。贴身那件软甲「嗤」地裂开，像一张泡烂的纸；肋下的骨头「咔」地断了，断的地方，一口气也吸不进去。水漫过他的耳朵，岸上的声音都隔了一层。白衣人蹲了下来，那张白得看不出年纪的脸，离他不到一尺，脸上没有怒，也没有喜，只有那一点笑，挂在嘴角上，像挂在井沿上的一层霜。他从袖子里摸出一面铜镜，跟马小宝那一面一般大，镜面朝下，慢慢地，贴到了他胸口的木牌上。

「在这里头。」那人道。说完，低低地笑了起来，笑得很耐心，像一个人找了很久的东西，终于摸到了，不急着拿。

木牌凉得像一块冰。小满想动，动不了；想喊，一张嘴，灌进来的是泗水。他瞪着眼，瞳仁缩成了两个针尖，眼睁睁看着那面镜子压在自己胸口上。他这辈子头一回知道，人是可以这么死的：不用刀，不用拳，一根指头，一面镜子，蹲在你跟前，像蹲着看一口井里有没有水。

木牌炸开了一团银光。

岸上要是有人，看见的只是渡口底下亮了一亮，像谁扔了一把碎银子在水里。小满看见的是她：银月从木牌里扑出来，没有化狐，没有化人，只是一团光，扑在那面镜子上。白衣人整个人往后飞了出去，飞过三丈，落进河心，砸起一片水。那团光在半空里一晃，薄下去，薄下去，薄得像冬天窗纸上的一层霜。她回过头来，看了他一眼，只说了一个字：

「跑。」

光一灭，木牌凉了。

他是爬上石阶的。断骨头那一边贴着石头，一级，一级，三百级，他不记得爬到了第几级，只记得每一级都是他自己的血。爬到一半，河心里有人站了起来。那人没追，站在齐腰深的水里，拿袖子擦了擦那面镜子，擦完了，往石阶上望着，嗓子还是平平的，从河面上贴过来，一个字也没散：

「跑什么。你找你的鼎。找着了，我来拿。」

小满爬上了最后一级，翻过山门，脸贴在石坪上。石坪是扫过的，干干净净，一片叶子也没有。他贴在那里，听着自己一口一口往里吸气，吸不进去，再吸。

他想起秘境里的邹青松。那一回，他的刀砍上去，一刀一刀全滑开了，可他至少看得清那人站在哪儿；这一回，他连那人怎么到他身后的，都没看见。那一回，她拔了两根毛；这一回，她把自己点着了。下一回——

没有下一回了。他得在下一回之前，长到她不用再点自己的地步。

回到观里，邓执事接过牌子，翻过来，背面写了一个「讫」字，底下钉上一块小牌，写了三个名字，头一个是沈小满。四块灵石放在柜台上，阿禾一块，孙二狗一块，他两块。邓执事看着他捂着肋骨的样子，道：「六层的东西。」小满道：「打的时候不知道。」邓执事道：「知道了，就不揭了。」

那天夜里，他在西廊那张铺上盘腿坐着吐纳。木牌贴在胸口，凉的，他捂了半夜，也没捂热。肋下那根骨头疼，他吸不深，只能一口一口地短着吸。吸到后半夜，丹田里那口缸底下忽然「咚」地一沉——不是丹，这一个月他没吃丹。沉下去的是芦苇里那一等：等它吸那一口气的那一霎。他六层了。

鯥的皮和翅膜，他在柴房里搁了一冬，腥气越搁越冲，西廊里三个师兄轮着骂了他一冬。转过年开春，他把那一卷子往饭桶跟前一放。饭桶没有鼻子，可它那只盖子一掀一掀的，分明是在闻；掀到第三下，盖子「哐」地一张，连皮带膜带捆的草绳，一口吞了下去，打了一个嗝，嗝里一股烤鱼味。

它闹了一夜肚子。咕噜咕噜，像一锅煮不开的粥，后半夜还「噗」地放了一个屁，满柴房的鱼腥。天快亮的时候，盖子一张，吐出一双鞋来。

那是一双丑鞋。灰褐色的矮靿靴子，鱼鳞的纹路一片一片还在皮面上，两只脚后跟上，各开着一道缝，像鱼鳃。鞋底上烙着三个字：**顺风溜**；底下一行米粒大的小字：「背后有风，脚下有路。」

那天夜里刮的是北风。小满穿上它，在柴房后头的空地上站定，灌一丝灵力进去——两只脚后跟上的「鳃」便张开了，「噗」的一声，像两只小兽打了个响鼻。他想了一想那行小字，背对着风，往后退了一步。

那一步退出去，人便起来了。不是飞——脚离地不过一尺，贴着地往前滑，像一片叶子贴着水面给风推着走，风从脚后跟那两道缝里灌进去，一滑便是十丈，到了墙根底下才停住。他转过身来，迎着风再试，那两道「鳃」张了张，「噗」，又「噗」，人一寸也没动。

衣襟里头，银月「哼」了一声——一冬了，这是她头一声，声音还薄，像隔着一层窗纸：「鱼皮鞋。还带响的。」小满站在墙根底下，半天没敢动，怕一动，这一声就没了。

他来来回回试了三回，丹田里便空了一半——六层的灵力，撑不住第四回。他坐在墙根底下喘气，心里明白了一样：这双鞋，不是打架的，是跑的。娘说过，打不过就跑；穿上这双鞋，跑之前，还得先看风。

祁长松是年三开春出的关。全观的人都在演武场上等着看，等出来的，还是一个九层：背上一身黑汗，臭的，人倒是囫囵的。有人上去问，他站在演武场边上，背着手，道：「这是头一回。」又道：「身子记下了，下回再来。」那年腊八，他又上了台，又拿了头名；转过年开春，第二回闭关，这一回，筑了基。观里便改口叫他祁师叔。

祁师叔头一回踩剑，是一个大清早，外门的人正在演武场上做早课。后山先起了一道青光，歪歪斜斜，像一只喝醉了的燕子。近了，才瞧清剑上站着一个人，方脸，两只脚死死踩着剑脊，身子往前压，跟当年在五行台上压人一模一样——可剑不是地，他越往前压，剑越往下扎。那剑在演武场上空兜了一个圈子，「哗啦」一声，一头扎进了东角那棵老柏里。

演武场上一百来个人，一个个憋得脸红脖子粗，腮帮子鼓得像蛤蟆，没一个敢笑出声。就是那一棵。前年腊八，一张画着猪的黄纸，拉着他撞上去的，也是这一棵。

伙房大娘拎着晾衣杆跑出来，跑到树底下，仰脸一瞧，是祁师叔，两只眼睛瞪成了两个铜钱，那根杆子便举不上去了：「……师叔，捅不捅？」树里静了一会儿，柏枝里头传出祁长松的声音，还是那么平：「捅。」

捅了三下，才捅下来。祁长松落了地，头发里插满了柏叶，活像一只刚出窝的刺猬，他拍掉一身的柏叶，把剑插回鞘里，一抬头，瞧见了人堆里的小满。他看了一会儿，道：「你那张猪，还有没有？」小满道：「……没了。」祁长松点点头：「可惜。它飞得比我稳。」说完，背着手走了，一步一步，走得极慢，脚底下踩得极实。

那一天，外门背着人笑了一整天：孙二狗蒙在被子里「哈哈哈哈」，笑一阵，捏着嗓子学一声「捅。」，又笑一阵。小满没笑。老柏的树皮上新撞掉了一块，白生生的，挨着前年那一块。一个人等一颗丹，等了二十年，冲了两回，头一回飞，落在树上。他自己呢，还在练气的半山腰上。

年五开春，那块青木牌还挂在西墙上。挂了两年，牌子长了一层绿霉，字还看得清：「寻我男人。沛县陈老四，腊月初二走的，去下邳贩布。」那块碎银子还拴在底下，没人动过。小满把它揭了下来。邓执事抬起头，道：「这块，工钱不够三个人的盘缠。」小满道：「我出。」他从怀里摸出两块灵石，放在柜台上。邓执事看了看那两块灵石，没拿，在簿子上写了三个名字。

沛县到下邳，贩布的走的是一条小道，翻两道梁。三个人走了三天，逢人便问，问到第三天，一个烧炭的老头说，大前年腊月那道梁上雪大，有个背布的在梁上歇过脚，后来没见他下来。人是在梁背后一道沟里寻着的——阿禾寻着的，她看地，看见沟边的草比旁处的绿。沟里剩的东西不多，一堆骨头，一副背架，背架上的布早烂成了泥；骨头旁边，一只布鞋，鞋底是纳的，针脚密，还没穿透。小满把那只鞋拿草叶擦了，包进油纸里。骨头他们埋了，阿禾在上头压了三块石头。

回到泗水，他没先去执事堂，先去了沛县西乡。那妇人在门口纳鞋底，看见他手里的油纸包，手停了。她没哭，把鞋接过去，翻过来看了看鞋底，看了很久，道：「是我纳的。」她进屋去，出来的时候手里攥着一块碎银子，跟牌子底下那一块一样大，往他手里塞。小满没接。她便站在门口，看着他走到看不见。邓执事把牌子翻过来，背面写了一个「讫」字，想了想，把底下那块碎银子解下来，放进簿子里压着，道：「这个，不算工钱。」小满道：「那算什么？」邓执事道：「算她的。」

那年秋天，他七层了。七层上，他卡住了。

卡住的不是缸——缸照旧涨，涨到半截，他照旧停。卡住的是剑。瞿老那年教的是入隙——「巽，入也」，这三个字他头一课就听过了，到七层才教。瞿老把一块青石搁在地上，道：「你砍它一剑。」小满一剑砍下去，火星子迸了一地，剑弹了回来，石头上一道白印子。瞿老拿扫帚把在石头上慢慢地摸，摸到一处，停住，拿扫帚把尖轻轻一点，那块石头便顺着一道看不见的缝，「啪」地裂成了两半。「石头也有缝。」瞿老道，「你没看见，不是没有。」他念了一句书：「《庄子》{典=zhuangzi-wuhou}里有个庖丁，宰了十九年牛，刀还跟新磨的一样。他说：『彼节者有间，而刀刃者无厚，以无厚入有间。』牛有缝，刀没有厚，拿没有厚的，进有缝的。」他把扫帚把一收，「鯥那一回，缝在肉上，眼睛看得见。往上走，碰上的东西，缝在灵力上。你的剑有厚，你看不见缝。」

看炉的牌子，他一直没交回去。丹房里，闵丹师那年教他碾药。碾药是坐在矮凳上，膝盖上一只铜碾船，一只脚踩着碾轮，来来回回。「黄精，碾到看不见丝。」闵丹师道，「当归，碾到闻不见甜。碾过了，药气跑了；碾不够，火进不去。」他碾了一冬，碾到闭着眼睛，手指头一捻，便知道哪一样碾到了哪一步。闵丹师从来不夸人，有一回拿起他碾的黄精闻了闻，没说话，倒进了炉里。那一炉出了三颗一纹的。闵丹师数完了纹，看了他一眼。

五年里的第三个秋天，阿禾十五，《阴符经》头一篇「生」，读到了头。观主把她叫进正殿后头的静室，从袖子里摸出一只小瓷瓶，倒出一颗丹，搁在她手心里，道：「今夜，吃了。」没有大比，没有名录，周衡的账上，也没有这一笔。她挑的是个没月亮的夜，锅盖云扣在正殿顶上，天是黑的，云也是黑的，全观没一个人抬头。观主在静室门外坐了一夜，天亮进去看了她一眼，只说了一句：「出了这扇门，你还是练气。」一个十五岁的天灵根筑了基，传到太一宫的耳朵里，她便不是沉鼎观的人了。

第二天傍晚，小满巡园巡到东角，照例在矮墙上坐下。阿禾蹲在那几棵禾跟前，掌心悬在土上，头也不回，道：「我筑了。」

小满道：「筑了什么？」话一出口，他自己便懂了。她还是那个背影，两根辫子，一件洗白了的袄；可他往她身上一看，从前看得见的那一点灵力，看不见了，像一盏灯，给人罩上了灯罩。

他先出来的是一声笑，真笑，笑得从矮墙上跳了下来：「真的？」阿禾道：「昨夜。」小满道：「疼不疼？」阿禾想了一想，道：「疼。比你大比那天疼一点。」她又低声补了一句，像怕地里听见：「还有一样。昨夜那一下，丹田里多了一穗谷。」小满低头看她的手：什么也没有，只有指缝里沾的一点土，在她话音落下的时候，轻轻拱了一下。她把手收进袖子里，没再说。

他还在笑，笑着笑着，心里有一处地方，轻轻抽了一下。大比那天他在台上一场一场地打，那只玉盒子到底是人家的；她那一颗，是从袖子里摸出来的。他知道这不怪她。他也知道，这一下抽，不是假的。

阿禾回过头来，看了他一眼。她看人一向准，这一眼也准。她把手从土里拿出来，在衣襟上擦了擦，一本正经地道：「我先上去，替你看看上头什么样。哪一级滑，哪儿有坑，一样一样记下来，等你上来，交给你。」顿了一顿，「收利息。」

小满道：「多少？」阿禾道：「还没算。你上来得越晚，利息越多。」

小满又笑了。这一回，一半是真笑，一半是认了。那天夜里，他在柴房里坐到蜡烛烧尽了，在黑地里小声道：「……利息，少算一点。」那年除夕，周衡照旧去正殿求了一回，观主照旧说外门里今年没人筑基，只多给了半句：「亲传，不算外门。」

On the hottest nights of the dog days, when the garden round was done, the three of them would sit on the herb garden's low wall to cool off: Xiaoman, A-He, Sun Ergou.

Xiaoman asked: "What would you like to be called?" Sun Ergou thought for a long time and said: "…Ergou still. My mother's used to it."

Xiaoman did not laugh. Nor did A-He. Under the wall the little Zheng rolled over and snorted.

Five years went by in a blink.

Shen Xiaoman's five years: roughly a layer a year. The storyteller takes the first three first — five, six, seven. The thick soil the pinch of earth had grown into: one breath in, one breath kept; the Rice Tub gave him one or two qi pills a month, and the odd three or four he put away and did not eat; at half a jar a layer he stopped, and filled the other half himself at night, breath by breath. His mother had explained his name: full, and it spills; fed a little, and you still know hunger.

The breath of the *Classic of Breathing* changed its shape with every layer. At five, a breath in and the jar could be heard — like water poured into an empty crock; at six the water stood higher, the sound was gone, and a breath out ran half as long again as a breath in; at seven the breath sank to the soles — his father's line in the snow, years ago, and only now did he learn how far it sank: to the heels.

The spirit stones, at first, he earned off the west wall of the Hall of Errands.

In the autumn of the third year he took down his first tag: The Spirit-Herb Valley north of Mount Meng, a monster by night, layer six, not yet awakened, eating the spirit-herbs and hurting people, twenty spirit stones each. Steward Deng looked at the tag, then at him. "Layer five?" "Layer five," said Xiaoman. "The monster is layer six — a layer above you. No one goes alone," said Steward Deng. "An errand tag takes three." Xiaoman looked round: two people stood behind him — Sun Ergou, layer one, who had tagged along to watch, and A-He, the herb garden's little hoe still in her hand. "I'll go," said A-He. "I'd like to see what kind of monster likes eating spirit-herbs." Steward Deng looked at her, said nothing, and wrote three names in his book.

The Spirit-Herb Valley lay north of Mount Meng, most of a day's walk; its fields all grew herbs the temple ordered, tended by a few herb-farming households and delivered once a year. The monster was real: after dark a thing would squat on the field dyke, rabbit-sized, with a bird's beak, a pair of round owl's eyes and a snake's tail, and the moment anyone came near it fell over and played dead; by dawn another patch of spirit-herbs was gone. The herb-farmers had hit it with hoes; it rolled over and ran, and the spirit-herbs went on vanishing; two of the night-watchmen were already hurt, one with a leg pecked through, one with a shoulder broken by the snake tail. The headman showed them a hoe handle: one gash, upper and lower beak right through, the break as clean as if snipped with shears. Xiaoman measured the width of the gash against his fingers and said nothing. A thing the size of a rabbit cannot open its jaws that wide; a thing that can is not chased off with hoes.

The three of them squatted on the dyke all night. After the third watch the thing came, hopping out of the spirit-herb rows, and the moment it saw a shadow it fell over belly-up, tail not even twitching. Sun Ergou, holding the lantern, bent over it a long while and whispered, "It's — it's asleep." Xiaoman nocked an arrow; A-He pressed his bow down. "Wait."

She crouched, not looking at the creature's belly but at its spirit-power. That lump of power was a muddy yellow with a green cast, drawn in tight; it did not look like a sleeper, it looked like a man hiding a fist behind his back. "Layer six, a wood foundation," she said under her breath. "The Classic of Mountains and Seas has it. Qiuyu. Sleeps at the sight of men." Xiaoman's finger tightened on the string: he was layer five.

The Qiuyu's eyelid moved.

It did not rise; it rolled over, landed on all fours, and in one bound was at Sun Ergou. He was still bent double, lantern raised, mouth open: "It — it—" The beak snapped shut on the lantern, which broke into three pieces; the oil sloshed out and flame ran along it and up his sleeve. He screamed and sat down hard on the dyke, in exactly the spot the snake tail could reach.

A-He's right hand had already formed an orchid seal and pointed at the dyke. Her spirit-power sank into the earth through the empty air, and three green vines shot out of the ground: two lashed round the hind legs and one cinched round the waist, pinning its hindquarters where it stood, so that it could only twist about, biting as far as its beak and tail could reach. It wrenched, and one vine snapped. "That thing is all brute strength," said A-He, her brows drawn tight, her right-hand seal unbroken, "I can't hold it for long!" Her left hand had already reached out, three zhang away, and pressed lightly on the air toward Sun Ergou's sleeve: a thread of green spirit-power flowed across, the flame lay down and went out, and the scalded skin under the cloth faded from red, bit by bit. "Don't move!" she shouted. "If you move I can't cover both!"

Xiaoman did not look at her; his feet had already moved. He had nine squares in his head — the first lesson of Old Qu's Heluo Sword, feet first, sword after — and now he stepped into the Xun place, left foot on the south-east square, the sword not out yet but the man already half a square aslant, the Matchstick's point hanging to the ground, brushing the mud: in the Xun trigram the broken line lies at the bottom, the soft thing underneath. A layer-five Matchstick, filled to the brim with spirit-power, a film of oil-light on its edge. His father used to say, the wind has to stop for breath. He waited.

Every square he trod lay on the edge of the circle it could reach; each vine that snapped made the circle a foot wider. The beak tore into the square he had just left — snap, clapping shut on nothing. He stepped to the next square. It went for his ribs; one more square. Bite after bite — it was faster than he was, much faster, but before every bite its eyeball moved first; each bite fiercer than the last, and shorter. The snake tail he could not dodge: one lash across his shin, like being struck with a whip, the trouser leg wet. Two more; three ridges swelled up one after another.

And that was when Sun Ergou moved. He saw the fire was out, scrambled up to run, blind with panic, and ran straight into Xiaoman's square. The sword-tip swerved; Xiaoman shouldered him aside with his left shoulder, and that cost half a step: the snake tail swept round with a crack and lifted Sun Ergou off the ground, three zhang through the air, and dropped him in the spirit-herb rows without a sound. Over there another of A-He's vines snapped. "Xiaoman," she said, her voice drawn tight, "Quick — I can't last long."

She loosened half a finger of her right hand; her left turned over toward Sun Ergou: green power ran along the furrow, and the huge purple bruise on his ankle faded little by little. He opened his eyes and groaned. A thin sweat stood on her brow and her breath came a little quick, her eyes never leaving the vines.

Then the last vine snapped.

Free of the bonds, it came down on him with its whole body, no longer biting one bite at a time but ramming — beak, tail and four claws at once. Xiaoman's nine squares fell apart: back to the right lay Sun Ergou, who had not got up yet; back to the left was the deep furrow of the herb rows, and if he fell back into it, Sun Ergou would lie wholly under its claws. Forward was its mouth; back was Sun Ergou's life. Both ways were dead ends. He drew half-circle after half-circle with the sword-point before him, guarding only, not daring to strike; the beak went past his neck and took a lock of his hair, the snake tail cracked across his waist, three squares back in one blow, the sword nearly gone from his hand.

"Hold on, Xiaoman!" shouted A-He. She let go of the vine seal, pinched a fresh sign with her right hand and pointed it under the Qiuyu, and the ground within three feet of its paws burst open and a great thicket of brambles shot up, the canes all barbed, the leaves edged with a ring of fine saw-teeth; the brambles crowded so close there was no gap to put a foot. One step and the barbs went into the flesh; one move and the saw-teeth drew a bloody line down a leg. Not one spirit-herb was touched. The Qiuyu slowed all at once: a claw lifted and came down, and every step it had first to pull its leg out of the brambles; it was a creature that lay down at the sight of men, and this time it could not even lie down — lie down, and it was all thorns.

This was the half-beat Xiaoman had been waiting for. His left hand pinched a sword-seal, two fingers swept from hilt to point, and he drew a thin thread of metal spirit-power from his dantian down his arm into the Matchstick. A pale gleam plated the dull red blade like frost on a copper kettle on a winter night; the edge went thinner and keener at once. The weakest of his five gates, and enough for this once.

He tapped his toe on the dyke beside Sun Ergou and rose straight off the ground, clean over the Qiuyu's head — stuck in the brambles it could not move, and could only lift its neck and watch a shape come down on it out of the moon. The plated Matchstick, point down, one white flash, went in at the back of its neck, in to the hilt. It did not even finish its cry, twitched twice on the blade, and was still. Still in mid-air, he could not keep his mouth shut: "Good thing my metal beats it."

Xiaoman came down — into A-He's great thicket of brambles. A-He's hand drew the spell back in the same blink that he landed, and the brambles shrank away with a whoosh, but a heartbeat late.

He fell flat on his back; the barbs caught his sleeves, the saw-teeth drew a few gashes across the back of his hand and his face, and the barbs' sharp tips stuck in his hand. The brambles were gone clean, and he scrambled up with a face full of little cuts, looked at A-He, held up his hand, and grinned: "What a terrifying spell!" He pulled a face. "I'll never dare make you angry again."

A-He, panting, looked up at him: "Good. Remember that." She stepped up, took hold of his wrist, pinched a seal with the other hand, and a layer of green spirit-power came through her palm, cool, like rain-washed leaves laid on the skin. The cuts on his hands and face closed over one by one, the beads of blood stilled, and the pain ebbed bit by bit; the welts on his calf and the bruise at his waist faded a shade. "Don't move," she said, stone-faced. "There are still a few thorns in the flesh. I'll pull them in a moment." Xiaoman sat very obediently and did not dare pull another face.

When the herb-farmers crowded round with torches, Xiaoman was sitting on the dyke, the cuts on his hands and face only just skinned over, his trouser leg slit open, three whip-welts on his calf swelling one by one and a deep beak-hole under them that A-He had only stanched — pecked at some moment he had never felt; and a great bruise at his waist. He took out a mending pill and swallowed it, and said: "It doesn't sleep." A-He crouched to look at his leg. "The book says it sleeps at the sight of men. The book doesn't say the sleep is a sham." She wrote that into her notebook.

At dawn the herb-farmers brought two strings of cash and a basket of eggs. The old herb-farmer also skinned the Qiuyu with a knife and brought out three things: a pair of owl's eyes, perfectly round and golden, that still glowed by torchlight; a beak, its edges sharp as shears; and a length of mottled snake-tail hide, soft and tough. "The eyes the apothecaries will buy, as a night-sight ingredient," said the old man. "The beak and the hide, you three share out." They shared them: the eyes to Xiaoman, who had killed it; the beak to A-He, who would take it back and add another line to her notes beside the Classic of Mountains and Seas; the tail hide to Sun Ergou, who had taken a tail-lash for everyone and deserved something. Sun Ergou hugged the hide and could not speak for a long while. Back at the temple Steward Deng turned the tag over — the character *done* on its back — and counted out sixty spirit stones, twenty to each of the three. A-He took her share without counting, and took out her little notebook to write a line. "What are you writing?" said Xiaoman. "Eggs. Twelve," said A-He. A pause. "Interest charged separately."

The storyteller will put in a word here: on this trip A-He saved all three of them, and Xiaoman won a duel with a sham sleeper — and won it ugly. The five years that followed went much the same — she read the ground, he read the quarry; she found the way, he struck; and the one who took the beating was Sun Ergou.

Twice a month on the clifftop Old Qu taught him the sword of Xun the fourth with a broom handle, and he followed with the Matchstick. Old Qu did not talk much when he taught: one form a layer, one sentence a form. In five years the cloth on the sword's hilt was changed three times.

In the spring of the fourth year he taught Going-with-the-wind. The wind was up on the clifftop that day; Old Qu stood on the Xun square with a leaf pinched in his fingers, let it go, and as it flew his broom handle went with it — the leaf east, the handle east, the leaf a turn, the handle a turn, neither fast nor slow, like a man walking a dog. "Still yourself, and you can see the wind rise," said Old Qu. "Seen it, don't meet it. Meeting is Gen; you are not a mountain. Go with it half the way and half its force is spent; the other half is yours." He recited a line: "The *Zhuangzi* says, 'Liezi rode the wind and went, light and well' — Liezi walked on the wind, and went so lightly. And a line further down: 'yet there was still something he depended on.' He still had to wait for the wind." He leaned the broom back in the corner. "This sword art borrows the wind. Borrow the wind, and however light you go, you must have wind. The patriarch left only half the scroll, as far as Core Formation; above that, what is wanted is the skill of borrowing nothing, and that is not in this half. Borrow it, for now." As he left he added one more, as if offhand: "What you can't cut through, don't cut. Wait for it to leak."

Going-with-the-wind he learned on the east bank of the Yi.

That autumn a red tag went up on the west wall: *East bank of the Yi: a bull-headed thing comes ashore at night; three plough-oxen dragged off. Four spirit stones.* A poor village's headman had posted it, the words written for him by the county clerk. The old hands gave it one look and left — four stones, three oxen, and nobody knew what the thing was: not worth it. It hung seven days. On the morning of the eighth Xiaoman took it down. "A red tag at layer five?" said Steward Deng. "Layer five may," said Xiaoman. Steward Deng looked at him a while, and wrote three names in his book.

He read the tag not for its words but for its tracks. Three oxen, and no blood mentioned — a thing the size of an ox, bitten to death by anything, leaves blood on the dyke; no blood meant not killed but dragged off alive; and dragged not into the hills but into the water. What drags off a whole ox? He thought about it all night and got nowhere. When you cannot work it out, do as his father did: first read the wind, then the deer; if you cannot see the deer, set your people in place first.

It was dark when the three of them reached the east bank of the Yi. The headman led them to the shore. The mud was a mess of hoofprints, and down the middle of them ran a drag mark two feet wide, from the ox-shed straight into the water; either side of it a line of claw prints, not deep, not shallow, and between the claw prints a wavering groove, like a thick rope hauled across mud. A-He crouched over the groove. "A snake's tail." She looked at the claw prints. "Four legs. Hooves." She opened her notebook to the back and read: "The *Classic of Mountains and Seas*, Southern Mountains, Mount Di: 'There is a fish there shaped like an ox, that lives on the hillside, with a snake's tail and wings, its feathers under its ribs, its voice like a lowing ox; it is called the Lu; it dies in winter and lives again in summer.'" "A fish?" said Xiaoman. "A fish that lives ashore, shaped like an ox, snake-tailed, with wings under its ribs. Dies in winter, lives in summer — it has to sleep as if dead through the winter, and before it sleeps it must eat its fill." She shut the book. "This is when it is hungriest."

"How big?" asked Xiaoman. "The book doesn't say. Big enough to drag an ox." The headman wanted to take men to guard the ox-shed; Xiaoman waved him off and sent the whole village indoors — doors barred, lights out. Sun Ergou unslung the pine board from his back — he had planed it himself behind the woodshed, taller than a man, with three iron bands nailed round it — and planted it across the mouth of the drag mark; he stood behind it, the torch stuck in the board's edge, lighting his face white and bright. A-He stood two paces behind him, her right hand lightly holding a seal, fingertips toward the mud of the shore. Xiaoman stayed out of the light; he backed twenty paces downwind, squatted in a clump of reeds, and laid the Matchstick across his knees.

It was the seventh tag they had taken that year. Nobody had to tell anybody anything.

When the moon came up, the water stirred.

The thing came up out of the water: first an ox's head, two horns, a pair of ox eyes glowing green in the torchlight; then a body, an ox's too, blue-black and oily-slick like a fish; behind it a snake's tail longer than its body, sweeping the shore. It was a size smaller than an ox. Once ashore it did not stop; head down, it charged straight at the torch — it saw nothing but that light, and the board beneath it.

Sun Ergou drove both feet into the mud, bent his knees and sank his seat. It was an earth stance Master Chu taught in the lecture hall, one every outer disciple had learned and hardly anyone took seriously: Mountain-Root Stance. In two years Sun Ergou had mastered nothing else, but he had mastered this — once he sank into it, his feet seemed to grow roots. Boom: the ox head struck the board. The board slid back three feet, ploughing two furrows in the mud — and stopped. Sun Ergou was still standing, his face squashed sideways by the board, shouting, "I'm a mountain… I'm a mountain…"

It backed a step and charged again; the board didn't move. But the snake tail came round the edge of the board and swept, whoosh, at Sun Ergou's ankles.

A-He pinched the orchid seal with her right hand and pointed it at the sweeping tail. A thicket of brambles burst up out of the shore, barbs turned outward; the tail swept into it and came away bristling with thorns. The brambles climbed the tail and up its hind legs, coil on coil, and drew tight. It heaved with the pain and could not break free — its head against the board, its hind legs pinned to the shore by brambles, it could go neither forward nor back.

The skin under its ribs opened — two wings, thin as a bat's, as big as a mat when spread. It meant to fly, to tear itself loose brambles and all. Before the wings spread it had to draw a breath, and as it drew, the skin at the wing root turned back — for an instant, pink flesh beneath, like a fish's gill.

That instant was what Xiaoman had been waiting for in the reeds. The little flying sword clipped between his fingers — he pinched the seal and let it go, and a streak of white skimmed low over the mud and went in through the pink flesh.

It bellowed like an ox, with a trailing note at the end like a man shouting under water; its wings half spread and sagged. It struggled a few times, then stopped, lying on its side among the brambles, one ox eye turned to the sky.

Only then did Sun Ergou come out from behind his board. His legs were too stiff to bend; he shuffled over step by step, sat down beside Xiaoman with a thump, and looked at his two hands — the iron bands on the board's edge had taken two patches of skin off his palms, bloody. A-He crouched and felt his wrist; a thread of power ran down through him from it. "The bones are fine," she said. A-He pinched a seal with her left hand; a thread of green light welled from her fingertips onto the wounds, and at once they were more than half healed. Sun Ergou looked at his palms, grinning: "Brother Shen, I — I held." Xiaoman said, "You held. It hit you twice." Sun Ergou said, "Three times." He held up three fingers. "You missed the first one. I was counting."

At daylight the headman brought the whole village down to the shore and they dragged it out of the brambles: a size smaller than an ox, its blue-black hide shining blue in the sun. The village ate meat for three days — it tasted of fish, and was not rank. The headman gave them a basket of eggs and a jar of wine. Xiaoman asked for two things: the membrane of the two wings under its ribs — thin, tough, clear against the sun, and it held the wind; and the hide off its back, uncommonly thick, which took the headman half a day to flay and rolled his knife-edge three times. He rubbed hide and membrane with salt, rolled them up, and carried them back up the mountain.

By the time they were back at the Si it was nearly dark. Sun Ergou had sat his stance half the night and his legs were still too stiff for the steps, so A-He held him up and took him up first; Xiaoman crouched in the shallows below the ferry to rinse the hide once more — the salt hadn't gone all the way in, it reeked, and carried into a west-wing room with four to a room it would earn him a cursing.

The river suddenly went quiet.

Not the wind dropping — the water stopping. The few strands of weed in the shallows, which had swayed with the current, now stood straight up, as if set in ice. The autumn insects on the bank, a whole chorus a moment ago, fell silent all at once. The moon lay on the water, and the water lay flat as a mirror, not a ripple on it. The token on Xiaoman's chest went cold for an instant, so cold his hand jerked, and the hide fell into the water.

"Fish skin," someone said behind him. "Good stuff."

The voice was dry and deep, like someone leaning over the mouth of an old well and calling down into it. Xiaoman didn't turn round; the hairs on the back of his neck rose one by one.

He snatched up Matchstick from the rock beside him and, without turning, sent the sword backward along the wind off the river. The man in white stood on the ferry steps, the moonlight on all that white making it look blue; one hand behind his back, and he didn't move. Half a foot short of his sleeve the sword-tip stopped, as if it had struck the surface of a well and could go not a hair further. Xiaoman's eyes went wide, his mouth hung open, a breath stuck in his throat — a thrust with all his power behind it, and before this man it could not so much as touch a sleeve.

The man laughed. Not loudly — a dry laugh, one note at a time, rising slowly as if from the bottom of a well, reaching the mouth, failing to scatter, sinking back. The sword sprang back on its own, jarring Xiaoman's hand numb and splitting the web of his thumb.

Xiaoman didn't try a second cut. He stepped back — a Yu step, left foot first, the right circling round — and the man was already standing behind him. He never saw him take a step. A chill crawled from the base of his spine to the back of his skull.

He pressed the escape talisman from his coat into his palm and pinched a seal — a flash of gold, and he was standing in the shallows three zhang away. He turned, and the blood drained clean out of his face: that white was right in front of him, as near as before, as far as before, not a drop of water on its hem.

"Three zhang," the man said, and laughed once more. "A good talisman."

One finger touched his chest, very lightly.

Xiaoman folded backward and lay down in the water. The soft armour against his skin split with a hiss, like paper gone to pulp; a rib under his arm snapped with a crack, and on that side not one breath would go in. The water closed over his ears, and every sound from the bank came through a layer. The man in white crouched down, that face so white it had no age a foot from his — no anger in it, no pleasure, only that trace of a smile hanging at the corner of the mouth like frost on a well's rim. He took a bronze mirror from his sleeve, the size of Ma Xiaobao's, face down, and slowly laid it against the token on Xiaoman's chest.

"In here," the man said. Then he laughed, low and patient, like a man who has groped a long time for something and at last has his hand on it, and is in no hurry to pick it up.

The token was as cold as a lump of ice. Xiaoman tried to move and couldn't; tried to shout, and when he opened his mouth it was the Si that poured in. He stared, his pupils shrunk to two pinpoints, and watched the mirror press down on his chest. For the first time in his life he knew that a man could die like this: no knife, no fist, one finger and one mirror, someone crouched in front of you, the way you crouch to see whether a well has water in it.

The token burst into silver light.

Had anyone been on the bank, all they'd have seen was a flash below the ferry, as if someone had thrown a handful of broken silver into the water. What Xiaoman saw was her: Yinyue flung herself out of the token — not as a fox, not as a girl, only a ball of light — onto the mirror. The man in white was thrown backward, flew three zhang, and came down in the middle of the river in a burst of water. The light wavered in the air and thinned, and thinned, thin as a frost on a winter window-paper. She looked back at him and said one word:

"Run."

The light went out, and the token was cold.

He crawled up the steps. The broken side pressed to the stone, one step, one step, three hundred steps; he didn't remember which step he had reached, only that every one was his own blood. Halfway up, someone stood up in the middle of the river. He didn't give chase. He stood waist-deep in the water, wiped the mirror with his sleeve, and when he had wiped it looked up at the steps, the voice still flat, sliding over the water, not one word frayed:

"Why run? You look for your cauldron. When you find it, I'll come and take it."

Xiaoman got over the last step, through the gate, and lay with his face on the stone terrace. The terrace was swept, clean, not a leaf on it. He lay there and listened to himself drawing breath, breath by breath, and it wouldn't go in, and he drew again.

He thought of Zou Qingsong in the secret realm. That time his knife had slid off, cut after cut, but at least he could see where the man was standing; this time he hadn't even seen how the man got behind him. That time she had pulled two hairs; this time she had set herself alight. Next time —

There would be no next time. Before next time, he had to grow to where she wouldn't need to set herself alight again.

Back at the temple Steward Deng took the tag, turned it over, wrote *done* on the back and nailed a small tag under it with three names, the first of them Shen Xiaoman. Four spirit stones on the counter: one for A-He, one for Sun Ergou, two for him. Steward Deng watched him holding his ribs. "A layer-six thing." "I didn't know that while I was fighting it," said Xiaoman. "Once you know," said Steward Deng, "you don't take the tag."

That night he sat cross-legged on his bunk in the west wing and breathed. The token lay against his chest, cold; he held his hand over it half the night and it never warmed. The rib hurt; he could not breathe deep, only short breath after short breath. Deep in the night the bottom of the jar in his dantian suddenly dropped with a thump — not a pill; he had eaten none that month. What dropped was that wait in the reeds: the wait for the instant it drew its breath. He was at layer six.

The Lu's hide and wing membrane sat in the woodshed all winter, stinking more the longer they sat, and the three senior brothers in the west wing took turns cursing him for it all winter long. In the spring of the next year he set the whole roll down in front of the Rice Tub. The Tub has no nose, but its lid lifted and lifted as if it were sniffing; on the third lift the lid gaped with a clang and swallowed the lot — hide, membrane and the straw rope round them — in one gulp, and burped, and the burp smelled of grilled fish.

It had a bellyache all night. Gurgle, gurgle, like a pot of gruel that wouldn't come to the boil; in the small hours it let out a pfft that filled the woodshed with fish-stink. Just before dawn the lid opened and it spat out a pair of shoes.

An ugly pair. Grey-brown low boots, the fish-scale grain still on the leather plate by plate, and a slit on each heel like a gill. Burned into the soles were three characters: Tailwind Slippers; and beneath, in letters the size of rice grains: "Wind at your back, a road at your feet."

That night the wind was from the north. Xiaoman put them on, stood still on the open ground behind the woodshed, and fed in a thread of qi — the "gills" on both heels opened with a pfft, like two small beasts snorting. He thought about the little line of writing, turned his back to the wind, and stepped back one step.

That step lifted him. Not flying — his feet no more than a foot off the ground, skimming forward like a leaf pushed across water by the wind; the wind poured into the two slits at his heels, and one glide carried him ten zhang, to the foot of the wall before he stopped. He turned round and tried again into the wind: the two gills opened — pfft, and pfft — and he didn't move an inch.

Inside his coat, Yinyue gave a little hmph — the first sound out of her in a whole winter, still thin, as if through a paper window: "Fish-skin shoes. Squeaky ones." Xiaoman stood at the foot of the wall a long while without daring to move, afraid that if he moved the sound would be gone.

He tried it back and forth three times, and his dantian was half empty — layer-six qi would not stand a fourth. He sat at the foot of the wall getting his breath back, and understood one thing: these shoes were not for fighting; they were for running. His mother had said it: when you can't win, run; in these shoes, before you run, read the wind.

Qi Changsong had come out of seclusion in the spring of year three. The whole temple was on the training ground to see, and what came out was still a layer nine: black sweat all down his back, rank, the man himself whole. When someone went up to ask, he stood at the edge of the training ground, hands behind his back, and said: "That was the first try." Then: "The body remembers. Next time I go again." That Laba he went up on the platform again and took first place again; the spring after, he went into seclusion a second time, and this time he laid his Foundation. The temple took to calling him Uncle-Master Qi.

Uncle-Master Qi's first ride was early one morning, while the outer court was at morning practice on the training ground. Over the back mountain a green light rose, slanting, like a drunken swallow. As it came near they made out a man standing on the sword, square-faced, both feet clamped to the blade's spine, leaning forward exactly as he had once pressed men across the platform — but a sword is not the ground, and the harder he pressed forward, the steeper the sword dived. It swung one circle over the training ground and, with a great rustle, went headfirst into the old cypress at the east corner.

A hundred-odd people on the training ground, every one of them red to the neck from holding it in, cheeks puffed out like toads, and not one dared laugh out loud. That tree. The Laba before last, a yellow paper with a pig drawn on it had dragged him into that very tree.

The kitchen auntie came running out with her laundry pole, ran to the foot of the tree, looked up, saw it was Uncle-Master Qi, her eyes went round as two copper coins, and she could not raise the pole. "…Uncle-Master — poke, or not?" Silence in the tree for a while; then out of the cypress boughs came Qi Changsong's voice, as level as ever: "Poke."

Three pokes, and down he came. Qi Changsong landed, his hair stuck so full of cypress sprigs he looked like a hedgehog fresh out of its nest, brushed off a coat of cypress needles, slid the sword back into its sheath, looked up, and saw Xiaoman in the crowd. He looked at him a while, and said: "That pig of yours — have you any left?" "…No," said Xiaoman. Qi Changsong nodded. "Pity. It flew steadier than I do." And he walked off, hands behind his back, step by step, very slowly, each foot set down very firm.

All that day the outer court laughed behind people's backs: Sun Ergou lay under his quilt going "Hahahaha!", laughed a while, pinched his voice to croak one "Poke.", and laughed a while more. Xiaoman didn't laugh. On the bark of the old cypress a fresh patch had been knocked off, raw white, right next to the one from the Laba before last. A man waits twenty years for a pill, pushes through twice, flies for the first time, and comes down in a tree. And he himself was still halfway up the slope of Qi Refining.

In the spring of the fifth year that green tag still hung on the west wall. Two years up, a skin of green mould on the wood, the words still legible: *Find my man. Chen Lao-si of Pei County, left on the second of the twelfth month, to Xiapi to trade in cloth.* The scrap of broken silver still hung under it; nobody had touched it. Xiaoman took it down. Steward Deng looked up. "That one — the pay won't cover the road for three." "I'll pay," said Xiaoman, and put two spirit stones on the counter. Steward Deng looked at the two stones, did not take them, and wrote three names in his book.

From Pei to Xiapi the cloth-traders took a footpath over two ridges. The three of them walked three days asking everyone they met, and on the third a charcoal-burner said the snow had lain deep on that ridge in the twelfth month three winters back, and a man with a cloth-pack had rested on the ridge and never been seen to come down. The man was found in a gully behind the ridge — A-He found him; she read the ground, and saw the grass at the gully's edge greener than elsewhere. Not much was left in the gully: a heap of bones, a carrying frame, the cloth on it long rotted to mud; beside the bones, one cloth shoe, the sole stitched, the stitches close, not yet worn through. Xiaoman wiped the shoe with grass and wrapped it in oilpaper. The bones they buried, and A-He set three stones on top.

Back on the Si he did not go first to the Hall of Errands but to the west of Pei County. The woman was at her door stitching a sole; when she saw the oilpaper packet in his hand, her hands stopped. She did not weep; she took the shoe, turned it over and looked at the sole a long time, and said: "I stitched that." She went in and came out with a piece of broken silver the size of the one under the tag, and pushed it into his hand. Xiaoman did not take it. So she stood at her door and watched him until she could not see him. Steward Deng turned the tag over and wrote *done* on the back, thought, untied the silver from under it and laid it in his book: "This one isn't pay." "Then what is it?" said Xiaoman. "Hers," said Steward Deng.

That autumn he reached layer seven. And at seven, he stuck.

It was not the jar that stuck — the jar rose as before, to the half, and as before he stopped there. What stuck was the sword. That year Old Qu taught Entering-the-gap — 'Xun is entering': he had heard those three words at his first lesson, and only at seven was it taught. Old Qu set a bluestone on the ground. "Give it a cut." Xiaoman cut down; sparks flew, the sword bounced back, a white mark on the stone. Old Qu felt slowly over the stone with the broom handle, stopped at one place, touched it lightly with the tip — and the stone split in two along a seam nobody could see. "Stone has seams too," said Old Qu. "That you didn't see one doesn't mean there isn't one." He recited a line: "In the *Zhuangzi* there is a cook, Ding, who butchered oxen for nineteen years and his knife was as if newly ground. He said: 'The joints have gaps, and the blade has no thickness; take what has no thickness into what has a gap.' The ox has seams; the blade has no thickness; take what has no thickness into what has a seam." He drew the broom handle back. "The Lu, that time — the seam was in the flesh, where eyes could see it. From here up, the things you meet have their seams in their qi. Your sword has thickness. You can't see the seam."

The furnace-watch tag he never gave back. In the pill house that year Pill-master Min taught him to grind. Grinding is done on a low stool, a bronze grinding-boat across the knees, one foot working the wheel back and forth. "Solomon's seal, grind till you can't see a fibre," said Pill-master Min. "Angelica, till you can't smell the sweetness. Grind too far and the virtue is gone; not far enough and the fire can't get in." He ground all winter, until with his eyes shut and a pinch between his fingers he knew which herb had reached which stage. Pill-master Min never praised anyone; once he picked up Xiaoman's ground Solomon's seal, smelled it, said nothing, and tipped it into the furnace. That batch gave three one-ring pills. Pill-master Min counted the rings, and looked at him.

In the third autumn of those five years A-He was fifteen, and she came to the end of "Birth", the Scripture's first chapter. The abbot called her into the quiet room behind the main hall, took a little porcelain bottle from his sleeve, tipped out a pill and laid it in her palm. "Tonight. Eat it." No contest, no register; and in Zhou Heng's ledger, no entry either. She chose a moonless night; the pot-lid cloud sat over the main hall's roof, the sky was black and the cloud was black, and not one person in the temple looked up. The abbot sat outside the quiet room all night; at dawn he went in, looked at her once, and said only: "Once you're out of this door, you're still Qi Refining." A fifteen-year-old heavenly root who had laid her Foundation — let that reach the Taiyi Palace's ears, and she would no longer be Chending Temple's.

The next evening Xiaoman's round brought him to the east corner, and he sat down on the low wall as usual. A-He was squatting by her few stalks, her palm held just above the soil, and without turning her head she said: "I've laid it."

"Laid what?" said Xiaoman — and the moment it was out, he understood. She was the same back as ever, two braids, a jacket washed pale; but when he looked at her, the little glow of qi he had always been able to see was gone, like a lamp someone had put a shade over.

What came out of him first was a laugh — a real one; he laughed himself right off the wall. "Truly?" "Last night," said A-He. "Did it hurt?" said Xiaoman. A-He thought about it. "It hurt. A bit more than you, the day of the contest."

He was still laughing, and somewhere in the middle of it something in his chest gave a small pull. On the day of the contest he had fought bout after bout on that platform, and the jade box was someone else's in the end; hers had come out of a sleeve. He knew it wasn't her fault. He knew, too, that the pull was not a pretend one.

A-He turned and gave him one look. She read people well, and she read this well too. She took her hand out of the soil, wiped it on her jacket, and said, perfectly straight-faced: "I'll go up first and see what it's like up there for you. Which step is slippery, where the holes are — I'll write it all down, and hand it over when you get there." A pause. "With interest."

"How much?" said Xiaoman. "Haven't worked it out," said A-He. "The later you come up, the more interest."

Xiaoman laughed again. This time half of it was a real laugh, and half of it was owning up. That night he sat in the woodshed till the candle burned out, and said softly into the dark: "…Go easy on the interest." That New Year's Eve Zhou Heng went to the main hall to ask as always, and the abbot said as always that nobody in the outer court had laid a Foundation this year — only this time he gave half a sentence more: "A personal disciple isn't outer court."
